§0Overview

How a fracture heals — the four stages

Bone is one of the few tissues that repairs itself with bone, not scar.

Where L4 named the types of fracture, this lecture answers the clinical question that follows: how does the break heal? Bone regenerates rather than scarring, so a healed fracture can end up as strong as the original. Secondary (callus) healing runs in four overlapping stages (Plate 0.1).

Label Key — Stages of fracture healing
Fracture haematoma
Blood from torn vessels clots at the break — the first, immediate response (0–1 days).
Periosteum
The vascular sleeve whose vessels and cells feed the repair; its intactness predicts healing.
New blood vessels
Angiogenesis brings oxygen and cells into the avascular clot — the rate-limiting step.
Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus
Cartilage + collagen bridge that splints the fracture but is not yet rigid (weeks 2–3).
Bony (hard) callus
Woven bone converts the soft callus into a solid bridge across the fragments.
Healed fracture (remodelled)
Remodelling restores the original contour and lamellar strength — ongoing for months.
Timeline of the four stages
StageWhat formsTiming
1 · HaematomaBlood clot + inflammatory responseImmediate (0–1 days)
2 · Fibrocartilaginous callusSoft (cartilage) callus bridges the gapReparative phase (2–3 weeks)
3 · Bony callusWoven bone replaces the soft callusReparative phase (weeks)
4 · Bone remodellingWoven → lamellar bone along stress linesOngoing (months–years)
Reasoning · why a blood clot has to come first

The haematoma is not just spilled blood — it is the scaffold and the signal box. Its fibrin meshwork gives cells something to crawl along, and the platelets and damaged cells trapped in it release the growth factors that summon everything else. No clot, no framework and no start signal — which is partly why anticoagulation and repeated disturbance of a fracture slow healing.

Clinical · secondary vs primary healing

The callus route shown here is secondary healing, which needs a little movement to stimulate callus. If a surgeon holds the fragments absolutely rigid (compression plate), bone can heal directly across the gap with no visible callus — primary healing. Choosing between them (cast vs plate) is a core fracture-management decision.

R Recall checklist — overview
  • Bone heals with bone, not scar — a healed fracture can regain full strength.
  • Four overlapping stages: haematoma → fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus → bony (hard) callus → remodelling.
  • Timing: haematoma 0–1 days; soft callus ~2–3 weeks; remodelling ongoing for months–years.
  • The callus route is secondary healing; rigid fixation gives primary healing (no callus).
§1Repair I

Setting the scene — the haematoma cascade

Bleeding and hypoxia flip on the switches that recruit the repair cells.

The first stage looks chaotic but is a tight signalling cascade (Plate 1.1). The clot's low oxygen and released factors do two jobs at once: grow new blood vessels and recruit stem cells that will become cartilage and bone.

Label Key — The repair cascade
Haematoma
The clot that fills the fracture gap — the starting point of the cascade.
Hypoxia
Low oxygen in the clot; the trigger that drives new-vessel growth.
VEGF → Angiogenesis
Hypoxia (via parenchymal cells) releases VEGF, which grows new blood vessels into the clot.
Platelets (thrombin activation)
Activated by thrombin; release growth factors that start the repair.
Immune cells
Clear debris and secrete cytokines that recruit more cells.
Cytokines / growth factors
The chemical calls that summon mesenchymal stem cells to the site.
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs)
Migrate towards and then within the fracture, then differentiate.
Chondrocytes / osteoblasts
The MSC offspring that will lay down cartilage (soft callus) and bone (hard callus).
Fibrin meshwork
The clot's scaffold — the surface cells crawl along to reach the gap.
Reasoning · why angiogenesis is the make-or-break step

Cartilage can form in low oxygen, but bone cannot — osteoblasts are hungry for oxygen and nutrients. So the whole repair hinges on hypoxia → VEGF → new blood vessels. Restore the blood supply and the cascade proceeds to bone; fail to, and it stalls at cartilage or dies — the direct route to nonunion. This is why blood supply is one of the two things that decide whether a fracture heals.

Clinical · what starves the cascade

Anything that blunts angiogenesis threatens healing: smoking (nicotine is a vasoconstrictor), peripheral vascular disease and diabetes, and fracture sites with intrinsically poor supply (the scaphoid waist, femoral neck). It is also why the periosteum — a key blood source — is protected during surgery wherever possible.

Memory hook · the two triggers

The clot shouts two messages: "I'm suffocating" (hypoxia → VEGF → vessels) and "send builders" (growth factors → MSCs → chondrocytes/osteoblasts). Vessels + builders = a callus can form.

R Recall checklist — repair I
  • Haematoma → hypoxia → VEGF → angiogenesis (new vessels invade the clot).
  • Platelets (thrombin) + immune cells release cytokines & growth factors.
  • Mesenchymal stem cells migrate to/within the fracture and differentiate into chondrocytes & osteoblasts.
  • The fibrin meshwork is the scaffold cells crawl along.
  • Blood supply is decisive — poor angiogenesis → nonunion.
§2Repair II

Callus formation — soft to hard

Cartilage lays the template; woven bone fills it; lamellar bone finishes it.

The recruited cells now build the bridge in two steps — first a soft cartilage callus, then a bony one (Plate 2.1).

§2.1Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus

Chondrocytes lay down cartilage across the gap. Crucially, this cartilage is a template for bone: it undergoes endochondral ossification — literally endo (inside) + chondral (of cartilage) + ossification (turning into bone). This is the very same mechanism that grew your long bones at the growth plate (see Bone Physiology I).

Label Key — Callus histology
Woven bone
New bone with irregular collagen orientation — laid down fast but weak.
Hyaline & fibrocartilage
The soft-callus template that bone replaces.
Endochondral ossification
Cartilage being converted to bone from within — the bridge between soft and hard callus.

§2.2Bony (hard) callus

Osteoblasts now lay down bone matrix, in two qualities that appear in sequence:

Woven vs lamellar bone in the callus
Woven boneLamellar (laminar) bone
Collagen fibresIrregular orientationRegular, ordered orientation
SpeedRapidly formedSlower — replaces the woven bone
StrengthWeakly load-bearingLoad-bearing
Reasoning · why build weak woven bone first

It is a speed-versus-strength trade-off. The body needs a splint now, so it throws down woven bone fast with its collagen in a disorganised felt — quick but weak. Once the fragments are bridged and stable, osteoblasts have time to replace it with lamellar bone, whose parallel collagen sheets are far stronger. It is the same 'rough draft then rewrite' strategy used in fetal ossification.

Memory hook · woven vs lamellar

Woven = weak & wild (fibres woven every-which-way, fast). Lamellar = layered & load-bearing (fibres in neat laminae). The callus goes wild → layered.

R Recall checklist — callus formation
  • Soft callus — chondrocytes make cartilage; the cartilage is a template undergoing endochondral ossification.
  • Endochondral = endo (inside) + chondral (cartilage) + ossification (turn to bone).
  • Hard callus — osteoblasts make bone matrix: woven bone first (irregular, fast, weak) then lamellar (regular, load-bearing).
  • Woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone as the callus matures.
§3Remodelling

Remodelling — the finishing stage

The bulky callus is sculpted back to the bone's original shape.

The bony callus is over-built and irregular. In the final, ongoing stage, the remodelling team you met in Bone Physiology I — osteoclasts resorbing and osteoblasts depositing — reshapes it into proper compact and spongy bone, restoring the original contour and strength.

Reasoning · why remodelling follows the lines of stress (Wolff's law)

Bone is laid down where it is loaded and removed where it is not — Wolff's law. During remodelling, osteoclasts strip away callus on the unloaded side and osteoblasts reinforce the loaded side, so the healed bone re-grows precisely along its mechanical stress lines. This is why controlled early loading (weight-bearing as advised) actually guides a fracture to heal in the right shape — and why remodelling can take months to years.

Clinical · children remodel spectacularly

A child's bone remodels so vigorously that even a fracture that heals slightly angled can straighten out over time — one reason paediatric fractures are often managed more conservatively than the same injury in an adult, whose remodelling is slower.

R Recall checklist — remodelling
  • Osteoclasts + osteoblasts reshape the bony callus into compact + spongy bone.
  • Remodelling follows Wolff's law — bone builds along stress lines, restoring contour & strength.
  • It is ongoing (months–years); children remodel far faster than adults.
§4Complications

When healing goes wrong — malunion & nonunion

Lose alignment and you get malunion; lose stability or blood supply and you get nonunion.

Two failure modes map neatly onto the two things healing needs. Lose alignment → malunion. Lose stability or blood supply → nonunion.

Malunion vs nonunion
MalunionNonunion
DefinitionFracture site is misaligned — bone heals with a change in angle or length.Fracture site lacks stability or blood supply — bone does not heal after 9 months.
TreatmentOsteotomy → fixation (e.g. ORIF — open reduction & internal fixation).External stimulation (e.g. ultrasound); internal stimulation (bone graft, BMP); fixation (ORIF).
ComplicationsReduced mobility · damage to surrounding structures · pain.Same as malunion · rare BMP-related heterotopic ossification.

Shared risk factors

  • Fracture-related — complicated fractures; delayed immobilisation; prematurely subjecting the bone to loads.
  • Patient-related — older age; lifestyle (poor diet, smoking); health conditions (diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, vitamin D deficiency).
  • Iatrogenic / other — medications (steroids, NSAIDs); infection.
Reasoning · why the risk factors are just 'stability + blood supply' in disguise

Read the list back through §1–§3 and it decodes itself. Delayed immobilisation, premature loading, complicated fractures = loss of stability. Smoking, diabetes, PVD, old age = loss of blood supply / angiogenesis. Poor diet, vitamin D deficiency = no building materials. Steroids/NSAIDs blunt the inflammatory-and-building signal; infection diverts it. Every risk factor attacks stability, supply or signal.

Clinical · the modifiable ones matter most

You cannot change a patient's age, but you can push the levers that decide healing: stop smoking, control diabetes, correct vitamin D and nutrition, minimise steroids/NSAIDs where possible, treat infection aggressively, and get the mechanics right (adequate immobilisation, sensible loading). BMP (bone morphogenic protein) can rescue a nonunion but rarely causes heterotopic ossification — bone forming where it shouldn't.

Memory hook · malunion vs nonunion

Malunion = healed badly (wrong angle/length). Nonunion = not healed at all (>9 months). Bad shape vs no join.

R Recall checklist — complications
  • Malunion — heals misaligned (wrong angle/length); treat with osteotomy → fixation (ORIF).
  • Nonunion — fails to heal after 9 months from lost stability or blood supply; treat with stimulation (ultrasound/graft/BMP) + fixation.
  • Risk factors reduce to stability, blood supply, materials or signal: smoking, diabetes, PVD, poor diet/vit D, steroids/NSAIDs, infection, premature loading.
  • BMP can rescue nonunion but rarely causes heterotopic ossification.
